stimulus.text: The third page of the engrossed Constitution, signed at Philadelphia on September 17, 1787, carries the end of Article II and the start of Article III. It says the person with the most electoral votes shall be President “if such Number be a Majority of the whole Number of Electors appointed,” and that if no person has a majority, “the House of Representatives shall in like Manner chuse the President” from the five highest on the list. Section 2 names the president “Commander in Chief of the Army and Navy of the United States” and gives power, “by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate, to make Treaties” and to appoint ambassadors and “Judges of the supreme Court.” Article III, Section 1 vests judicial power in “one supreme Court,” and says judges “shall hold their Offices during good Behaviour” and that their pay “shall not be diminished during their Continuance in Office.”
stimulus.source_note: Constitution of the United States, third page, engrossed by Jacob Shallus, signed September 17, 1787. Public domain.

stem: According to the page, which of the following can the president do only with the Senate’s agreement?

options.misconception: The page names the president commander in chief with no Senate role attached.

options.text: Grant pardons for offences against the United States
options.misconception: The page gives the pardon power with no Senate role attached, except in cases of impeachment.

options.text: Receive ambassadors and other public ministers
options.misconception: The page lists receiving ambassadors among the president’s own duties in Section 3.

rationales.A: The page says the president may make treaties “by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate,” with two-thirds of senators present concurring.
rationales.B: Commander in chief is listed as the president’s own power, with no Senate agreement needed.
rationales.C: The pardon power is listed without a Senate role, except that it does not reach cases of impeachment.
rationales.D: Receiving ambassadors is listed in Section 3 as the president’s own duty.
rationales.general:
1. Section 2 on the page lists the president’s powers one by one.
2. Treaties carry the words “by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate.”
3. Commanding the armed forces, granting pardons, and receiving ambassadors carry no such words.
4. So treaties are the power on the list that needs the Senate’s agreement.
Remember: “advice and consent” in the text is the mark of a shared power.
